title: What happens if a permitted subclass has no `final`/`sealed`/`non-sealed` modifier?
shortTitle: What happens if a permitted subclass has no `final`/`sealed`/`non-sealed` modifier?

s1_definition.profdef: It is a compile error. Every class or interface that directly extends or implements a sealed type is required to specify its own extensibility by being declared exactly one of `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`. If a permitted subclass omits all three modifiers, the compiler rejects the code with an error stating that a sealed class's subclass must be final, sealed, or non-sealed. The one exception is records and enums, which are implicitly final and therefore satisfy the rule automatically. This requirement forces the author to make a deliberate decision about whether the sealing continues, ends, or is reopened at each subtype.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India approves a product to be a kind of Account. Head office insists that each approved product must stamp its own policy on further variations: either "no further variants allowed" (final), "only my own named variants allowed" (sealed), or "anyone may add variants freely" (non-sealed). A product that forgets to stamp any policy is sent back — the form is incomplete, and head office refuses to file it. The bank will not accept an approved product that leaves its extension policy blank.
s1_definition.oneliner: A permitted subclass must declare `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`; omitting all three is a compile error, because sealing requires an explicit extensibility decision at every subtype.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** It is a compile error. Every class or interface that directly extends or implements a sealed type is required to specify its own extensibility by being declared exactly one of `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`. If a permitted subclass omits all three modifiers, the compiler rejects the code with an error stating that a sealed class's subclass must be final, sealed, or non-sealed. The one exception is records and enums, which are implicitly final and therefore satisfy the rule automatically. This requirement forces the author to make a deliberate decision about whether the sealing continues, ends, or is reopened at each subtype.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India approves a product to be a kind of Account. Head office insists that each approved product must stamp its own policy on further variations: either "no further variants allowed" (final), "only my own named variants allowed" (sealed), or "anyone may add variants freely" (non-sealed). A product that forgets to stamp any policy is sent back — the form is incomplete, and head office refuses to file it. The bank will not accept an approved product that leaves its extension policy blank.

**One line to remember:** A permitted subclass must declare `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`; omitting all three is a compile error, because sealing requires an explicit extensibility decision at every subtype.

sections.s2_technical:
When a type is sealed, it closes its hierarchy at the first level by naming its permitted subtypes. But sealing must not leak: if a permitted subtype could be extended freely without saying so, the hierarchy would no longer be closed, because unknown classes could slip in beneath that subtype. To prevent this, Java **requires every permitted subtype to state its own extensibility** explicitly, choosing exactly one of three modifiers.

**`final`** ends the hierarchy at that subtype: no class may extend it, so that branch of the closed family is a leaf. This is the most common choice for concrete products. **`sealed`** continues the closure: the subtype itself becomes sealed and must provide its own `permits` list (or rely on same-file inference), extending the closed hierarchy another level. **`non-sealed`** deliberately reopens that branch: the subtype may be extended by any class without restriction, punching a controlled hole in the sealing where you have decided extensibility is desirable, such as a base for third-party plugins.

If a permitted subtype **omits all three**, the compiler emits an error like "sealed, non-sealed or final modifiers expected." The compiler cannot guess your intent — leaving it blank would create an ambiguous, half-open hierarchy — so it forces the decision. This is a deliberate language design choice that makes extensibility an explicit, reviewed property of every subtype rather than an accident.

The important **exceptions** are types that are already implicitly final. A **record** is implicitly `final`, so a record that implements a sealed interface satisfies the rule without writing `final`. An **enum** is effectively final as well (its constants are fixed), so an enum implementing a sealed interface is fine. In these cases you do not add a modifier because the type's nature already closes it. For ordinary classes and interfaces, though, you must write one of the three.

A subtle point for **interfaces**: a sealed interface's permitted subtype that is itself an interface must be `sealed` or `non-sealed` (interfaces cannot be `final`), while a permitted subtype that is a class follows the class rules of `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`. So the exact allowed modifier set depends on whether the subtype is a class or an interface, but the principle is identical: the extensibility must be explicit.

A senior nuance is that this requirement is what makes the **closed-set guarantee hold transitively**: because every subtype must declare final, sealed, or non-sealed, the compiler can compute the complete leaf set for exhaustiveness checking, and a `non-sealed` branch is the one place where that set becomes open, which the compiler accounts for by then requiring a `default` or wildcard when switching if the open branch is reachable. Another nuance is that forgetting the modifier is a frequent first-time error, and the fix is simply to decide and declare it. A final nuance is that in a banking domain this explicitness is valuable because it forces an architectural decision at each product type about whether future variants are allowed, which is exactly the kind of deliberate design a regulated system benefits from.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A developer at National Bank of India writes a permitted subclass of the sealed `Account` but forgets to add any extensibility modifier, and the build fails. We need to show the error and explain that the compiler is forcing a deliberate decision, so the team learns to always declare one of the three.

Problem 2 — The team then decides the correct policy for each product: savings and current are leaves and must be `final`, loan has further sub-products so it is `sealed`, and one promotional line must stay open for future add-ons so it is `non-sealed`. We implement each with the right modifier.

Problem 3 — The team uses records for some immutable value-style results and learns that records satisfy the rule automatically because they are implicitly final, so no modifier is needed there. We show a record subtype of a sealed interface compiling cleanly.

In the mini-project we define a sealed `Account` with correctly-modified subtypes (final, sealed, non-sealed), show in comments the compile error from omitting the modifier, add a record implementing a sealed interface to demonstrate the implicit-final exception, and log usage.

The code contains: a sealed `Account`, final, sealed, and non-sealed subtypes, a sealed interface with a record subtype, and a demo.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile (Java 17+)
javac -d target/classes src/main/java/com/bank/modrule/ModifierRuleDemo.java

# If any permitted subclass omits final/sealed/non-sealed, javac fails:
#   error: sealed, non-sealed or final modifiers expected

# Run
java -cp target/classes com.bank.modrule.ModifierRuleDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a savings account, a home loan, a promo account, and a settled-trade record.

Step 1 — The compiler checks every permitted subtype of the sealed `Account`. Each one declares exactly one extensibility modifier, so compilation proceeds. The comment shows that if `SavingsAccount` had omitted `final`, the compiler would stop with "sealed, non-sealed or final modifiers expected," forcing the decision.

Step 2 — `SavingsAccount` is `final`, so its branch ends there; nobody can extend it, keeping that part of the family closed. The code creates one and logs its id and balance.

Step 3 — `LoanAccount` is `sealed`, so it continues the closure and provides its own `permits` for `HomeLoan`, which is a `final` leaf. The code creates a `HomeLoan`, showing a two-level closed hierarchy where each level declared its policy.

Step 4 — `PromoAccount` is `non-sealed`, deliberately reopening that branch for future unrestricted extension. The code creates one, demonstrating the controlled hole in the sealing.

Step 5 — Finally, a `SettledTrade` record implements the sealed `Settlement` interface. Because records are implicitly final, it satisfies the modifier rule without any keyword, and it is created and logged. This shows the record exception to the explicit-modifier requirement.

```
  final          sealed                     non-sealed
  SavingsAccount  LoanAccount                PromoAccount
  (branch ends)   permits HomeLoan           (branch OPEN)
                     │

  Record exception:
     sealed interface Settlement permits SettledTrade
        record SettledTrade implements Settlement   ← implicitly final, no modifier
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
If a permitted subclass has no final, sealed, or non-sealed modifier, it is a compile error. The language requires every class or interface that directly extends or implements a sealed type to declare its own extensibility by being exactly one of those three, and leaving all three off produces an error saying sealed, non-sealed, or final modifiers are expected. The compiler refuses to guess my intent, so it forces a deliberate decision at every subtype.

The reason is that sealing must not leak. A sealed type closes its hierarchy at the first level by naming permitted subtypes, but if one of those subtypes could then be extended freely without saying so, unknown classes could slip in beneath it and the hierarchy would no longer be closed. So each permitted subtype states its policy: final means the branch ends there with no further extension, sealed means it continues the closure with its own permits list, and non-sealed means it deliberately reopens that branch for unrestricted extension, which is a controlled hole I use for something like a plugin base.

There is an important exception I always mention: records and enums are implicitly final, so a record or enum that implements a sealed interface satisfies the rule automatically without any modifier. In my banking project I use a record for a settlement result that implements a sealed settlement interface, and it compiles cleanly with no extra keyword because it is already final. For ordinary classes and interfaces, though, I must write one of the three, and for a permitted subtype that is itself an interface the choice is sealed or non-sealed because interfaces cannot be final.

In my account model savings and current are final leaves, loan is sealed with its own permitted home-loan leaf, and a promotional line is non-sealed so it can take future add-ons. The value of this rule in a bank is that it turns extensibility into an explicit, reviewed architectural decision at each product type rather than an accident, and it is exactly what keeps the closed-set guarantee holding transitively so my exhaustive switches stay sound. So the short answer is: declare final, sealed, or non-sealed at every permitted subtype, or the build fails, and that is by design.

---

keyPoints: sealed: restrict which classes can extend/implement
permits: explicit list of allowed subclasses
Subclass must be: final, sealed, or non-sealed
Enables exhaustive switch/pattern matching — compiler checks all cases
